_Missourians should vote NO on Amendment 5 in the August 4 primary election. Please share this article with other voters and encourage them to vote. It 'll be a low-turnout election; every vote matters._
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=201207909&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjAxMjA3OTA5LCJpYXQiOjE3ODExODE3ODMsImV4cCI6MTc4Mzc3Mzc4MywiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.V--1RkMGeuRB1w0KpQ6fjZItNicELpNF7xKp1NPn4-4)
* * *
Missouri's election calendar is a bit unusual this year. For the first time since 2014, there are no marquee statewide candidate elections: no gubernatorial races and no U.S. Senate races.1
That means two things:
1. Because there aren't marquee candidate elections, turnout will likely be low.
2. For most Missourians,2 the votes they cast on ballot measures will be their most consequential.

On the August 4 ballot, two ballot measures are the most alarming and most profoundly threaten the state:
* **[Amendment 4](https://substack.com/redirect/01615f82-a1bd-4a09-b2d5-45c2ab94d7f5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , which would functionally end the right that Missourians have to initiate legislation and constitutional amendments via ballot measure, a critical check on the legislature.
* **[Amendment 5](https://substack.com/redirect/b9caea95-39fd-4523-9932-245174882709?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , which would abolish the state's income tax.

**Missourians should vote "no" on both**. In my next post, I'll write more about Amendment 4, which is a pretty clear-cut and brazen power grab.
Amendment 5 is more nuanced. Lowering taxes is a worthy goal, but **for most Missourians, Amendment 5 would drive their taxes** _**up**_**, not down**.
What's more: Missouri is far more reliant on its income tax revenue than most states, and the state has no cogent plan to replace the lost revenue. It would obliterate the state's budget and require substantial cuts to infrastructure, public safety, and health. We risk reducing these investments to some of the lowest levels in the country.
[Subscribed](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9iZW5zYW11ZWxzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MjAxMjA3OTA5LCJzIjoyNDQwMzk4LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1Ijo5MDUwMTE5MiwiaWF0IjoxNzgxMTgxNzgzLCJleHAiOjIwOTY3NTc3ODMsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0wIiwic3ViIjoibGluay1yZWRpcmVjdCJ9.poCo__msHIv9pmggEHv2UDt9cbESbfWzn_ESjaI6_tM?)
### Amendment 5 is rushed, incomplete policy that would obliterate Missouri's budget
Conceptually, I have no problem with Missouri trying to repeal its income tax. The problem is not the concept; the problem is the implementation.
The state legislature rushed the policy to the voters, and as a result, **Missouri has absolutely no plan for how it 'll pay for its services**.
To begin with, Missouri is unusually reliant on its income tax relative to other states. By eliminating its income tax, the state would forfeit more than 50% of its tax revenue.3
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/30c9b8c7-5065-4d94-8bda-c6fcc0bebeda?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [Tax Policy Center](https://substack.com/redirect/fb1ad169-cdec-4e76-a799-49c6e6102d8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), 2022. Missouri is highlighted in yellow.
OK, so if Missouri is about to get rid of more than 50% of its tax revenue, what's its plan to actually run the state? In short, there isn't one.
Is Missouri slashing its budget in preparation? Nope. They're doing the opposite. Missouri's budget has ballooned in the last six years, and while some of that is attributable to inflation, even against that baseline, the state is spending far more out of its general fund than it did before the pandemic.4
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/4b661429-4a8b-42a4-b816-aa02d02a3ea8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [Urban Institute](https://substack.com/redirect/a83de385-36db-4b63-bfb8-586dce1d81eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); [US Inflation Calculator](https://substack.com/redirect/a65b0adf-a14e-48d7-8fe5-92c7a048d09d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The whole premise of the proposed constitutional amendment is, basically, "we'll figure out how to deal with budget shortfalls if this thing passes." Here's how [Amendment 5 would change the state constitution](https://substack.com/redirect/73040f94-fcad-4061-a505-ef5ed4d7d2e5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) (emphasis added):
> 2\. (1) Notwithstanding any provision of this constitution to the contrary, including subsection 1 of this section, **for the purpose of reducing and eliminating the state individual income tax and reducing local tax rates, state and local sales and use taxes (or any similar transaction-based tax) may be expanded by legislation** to impose taxes on transactions involving any goods and services.
Using sales taxes to backfill the revenue lost from abolishing the income tax is a ridiculous proposal. For context:
* [Missouri collected $3.2 billion in sales tax revenue](https://substack.com/redirect/2b90c9ff-ab2b-4a28-bd65-aea1780c8bd5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in FY2025, 24.0% of the state's general revenue collections.
* Missouri collected $9.17 billion in individual income tax revenue in FY2025,5 68.3% of the state's general revenue collections.6

What on earth is the plan here? Already, [Missouri has the 12th-highest sales tax rate](https://substack.com/redirect/83713ad2-ad83-4219-af3b-967972cfb3de?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in the country. Economically, you can't just go out and triple the sales tax rate; that'd devastate restaurants and retail businesses, whose sales would be hurt by what would amount to a 10%+ increase in prices.
### For most Missourians, Amendment 5 will _increase_ their taxes
In any event, it's a political nonstarter. What legislator is going to support a plan to make Missouri the highest sales-tax state in the country? Not for nothing, [sales taxes are regressive](https://substack.com/redirect/28efc9a3-f5d4-4ce3-80fb-4e0388e9642f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg): while top earners spend less than 1% of their income on sales taxes, the bottom 20% of earners spend nearly 5%.7 As a result, **for most Missourians --[as many as 80%](https://substack.com/redirect/e163e4b3-4a48-42ed-b1de-99d1946c6ea6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--Amendment 5 will result in their effective tax rate going **_**up**_.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=201207909&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjAxMjA3OTA5LCJpYXQiOjE3ODExODE3ODMsImV4cCI6MTc4Mzc3Mzc4MywiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.V--1RkMGeuRB1w0KpQ6fjZItNicELpNF7xKp1NPn4-4)
To put this as bluntly as I can: **Mike Kehoe and the state legislature have no idea what they 're doing with this proposal**.
1. They're slashing the vast majority of state tax revenues without starting to meaningfully cut the budget.
2. They're trying to replace income tax revenue with sales and use taxes, which isn't politically feasible and isn't economically feasible.
3. Because Missouri has a [constitutional mandate to balance the budget](https://substack.com/redirect/d5f6afb5-eae2-405b-b8c9-c87177df908b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), they can't just start running deficits.

It's the definition of delusional, wishful thinking.
### Already, Missouri's government is underinvesting in the state. Amendment 5 would make things much worse.
By Missouri's own definitions, [74% of the money spent from Missouri's general revenue](https://substack.com/redirect/8ca7489d-06a9-4447-ac9c-dd422452cf42?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) is "mandatory."8 But even the so-called "discretionary" money in the state budget seems hardly discretionary: money to the Department of Transportation, Department of Public Safety, and Department of Corrections are all considered "discretionary" spending.9
Yes, Missouri does have its inefficiencies, and more serious policymakers would address government bloat throughout the state.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/2aed05d0-de4d-4a98-aede-88aa09ee57ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)| | |
#### [Missouri's insanely bloated government(s)](https://substack.com/redirect/2aed05d0-de4d-4a98-aede-88aa09ee57ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
---
| | [Ben Samuels](https://substack.com/profile/12425779-ben-samuels)| | *
---|---|---
| April 8, 2025
| [| Read full story
---](https://substack.com/redirect/2aed05d0-de4d-4a98-aede-88aa09ee57ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
But Amendment 5 doesn't pair responsible cuts in Missouri's spending--cuts that certainly exist--with tax cuts. It's simply saying that the state will surrender its largest source of revenue, and state legislators will have to figure out what to do with that.
First of all, it'll be open season for Jefferson City lobbyists. Companies, industry groups, and organizations will want to make sure that _their_ funding isn't cut. Groups with the strongest connections to Jeff City legislators will come out ahead at the expense of the rest of the state.
There are lots of places where _more_ government funding--or at least better government funding--would go a long way. There's a lot that Missouri needs to address:
* 30% of Missouri's school districts are [down to four days per week](https://substack.com/redirect/1f9baba9-a47c-4572-ab30-3213296b75ec?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
* Missouri ranks among the worst states in the country when it comes to [road condition](https://substack.com/redirect/b5fb6336-4edc-4c4c-8397-36b86a61c3c3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and [bridge condition](https://substack.com/redirect/a6493b4a-8a6f-463d-a765-b8ce42f11da3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
* Missouri has the [ninth-highest rate of drug use](https://substack.com/redirect/e4dfee41-e9f7-4212-9e99-8e8e1b05e89a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and [11th-lowest life expectancy](https://substack.com/redirect/7dc946a5-504c-4bbd-843a-dcf23d6f8906?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of any state in the country.
* Missouri has a [worse-than-average maternal death rate](https://substack.com/redirect/ca9a1f98-ec1b-4b16-9431-8ea50a2eb679?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and per state data, [77% of all pregnancy-related deaths](https://substack.com/redirect/954a9631-c9a4-4114-9bd2-fafa85c7c58c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) were preventable.
* Missouri is [48th in average teacher salary](https://substack.com/redirect/3600d78d-bde4-4dad-ad08-9451a4845bd5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

I'm not saying that throwing money at these problems will immediately make them better. But Amendment 5 would almost certainly result in large cuts to the state budget, and these are the sorts of programs--designed to help children, the poor, and the not powerful--that will be the first ones on the chopping block.
### No, tax cuts alone don't magically guarantee growth
The argument that the [Rex Sinquefield-funded proponents of Amendment 5](https://substack.com/redirect/1d6db91d-8a6e-40ff-83c4-052ac42e833e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) are making is that Missouri has to cut its income tax to keep from falling behind. Missouri Promise, the advocacy group in favor, has been [running this ad](https://substack.com/redirect/f0a89214-f1b4-41d2-88ea-1e6ef89a535c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), trying to hammer home that point.10
[](https://substack.com/redirect/ee40b458-b022-472f-9be4-9fe84804c633?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The ad is easy enough to understand: we're in a race with other states, and we're falling behind. But the whole premise is wrong. Getting rid of our income tax won't suddenly give us Tennessee's growth rate.11
All things held equal, it is better to be a state with lower taxes. But there are a million other things that factor into a state's growth and prosperity. Educational attainment, for instance, is [far more important in driving economic growth](https://substack.com/redirect/ee385d9a-51d7-453e-95f9-3c453b3af1e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) than tax policy.12 There are innumerable other factors that matter too: things that the government can impact (e.g., [housing costs](https://substack.com/redirect/3ae9c5d9-5e38-4e5b-b926-fce431f3c1e3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)) and things that it cannot (e.g., culture, [weather](https://substack.com/redirect/b68c5a0b-3efa-4672-876b-0592b13e2511?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)).13
Missouri _should_ aspire to lower its income tax rate, to lower its tax rates across the board, and to get more out of the money that the state spends. But **this is a sloppy, rushed effort that will result in the vast majority of Missourians dealing with higher taxes** and a hamstrung government delivering worse services for its residents.
### Kansas already tried this. It spectacularly failed.
Fourteen years ago, Kansas passed [HB 2117](https://substack.com/redirect/92e4bfd2-bfc0-482c-9b60-69c88ff4e0d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), in what became known as the "[Kansas experiment](https://substack.com/redirect/ed3f91c1-f0a0-45c4-a2ce-25ac1d9842d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)."
Kansas Governor [Sam Brownback](https://substack.com/redirect/9b90b90e-ad64-4573-939c-d02e12fc3f0a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) reduced the state's income tax, making a similar argument: cutting taxes would drive growth in the state that would outpace any necessary cuts to the state budget.
It was, by all measures, an unmitigated disaster. [Here's what happened](https://substack.com/redirect/81f85f35-7349-41d3-82cc-dedd8e4b9524?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg):
> Since the 2012 tax cut, however, Kansas's economy has lagged behind neighboring states and its budget has been in tatters. Lawmakers were forced to make significant cuts in vital programs such as [Medicaid](https://substack.com/redirect/c3d187f3-e491-4cd3-8638-60d5e0211b53?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), education, welfare, court funding, and infrastructure. [In 2017]--in the face of slow growth, two downgrades of Kansas's bond ratings, and a budget shortfall of almost [$900 million](https://substack.com/redirect/b4df3a8d-5d75-4fb9-8dab-c69649bb226b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--the state's Supreme Court mandated that Kansas increase education spending. And the Republican-led legislature reversed much of Brownback's original tax cut.
Given the scale of the proposed budget cuts in Missouri, the impact on the state would be even more extreme. To use a quote [misattributed to Albert Einstein](https://substack.com/redirect/6d818e81-b545-436c-9e1b-1db0e64d2ee2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), "the definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting a different result."
By this definition, Missourians would be insane to pass Amendment 5.
[Subscribed](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9iZW5zYW11ZWxzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MjAxMjA3OTA5LCJzIjoyNDQwMzk4LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1Ijo5MDUwMTE5MiwiaWF0IjoxNzgxMTgxNzgzLCJleHAiOjIwOTY3NTc3ODMsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0wIiwic3ViIjoibGluay1yZWRpcmVjdCJ9.poCo__msHIv9pmggEHv2UDt9cbESbfWzn_ESjaI6_tM?)
_**Share this post with Missourians and encourage them to vote in the August 4 primary election.** If you're reading this email because someone sent it to you, [please consider subscribing](https://substack.com/redirect/c09820e6-2990-4a98-b3f2-91e778c66717?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)._
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=201207909&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjAxMjA3OTA5LCJpYXQiOjE3ODExODE3ODMsImV4cCI6MTc4Mzc3Mzc4MywiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.V--1RkMGeuRB1w0KpQ6fjZItNicELpNF7xKp1NPn4-4)
1
The only statewide candidate race is the rather sleepy [election for State Auditor](https://substack.com/redirect/4292df7c-9df2-416c-88cc-571e33ec4270?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
2
One exception: the [Wesley Bell vs. Cori Bush rematch](https://substack.com/redirect/259a3e28-243a-41e1-945a-842103188f95?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in MO-01.
3
The story is more complicated when you look at income tax as a percentage of general revenue:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/014028c0-dc50-4a3a-b644-48416dea992e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [Tax Policy Center](https://substack.com/redirect/fb1ad169-cdec-4e76-a799-49c6e6102d8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), 2022. Missouri is highlighted in yellow.
General revenue includes non-tax money that the state gets: most notably transfers from the federal government, but also things like tuition to public universities. Even so, Missouri is still far more reliant on its income tax revenue than the average state.
It should also be noted that the data in this graph is from 2022, the last year I could readily find good information from the [Tax Policy Center](https://substack.com/redirect/fb1ad169-cdec-4e76-a799-49c6e6102d8f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). While there have been some changes--New Hampshire, for instance, [repealed its interest and dividends tax](https://substack.com/redirect/c5740e96-bf28-48b1-8be6-ba08022596a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--the state-to-state story is substantively similar.
4
As above, because of federal spending, the chart above doesn't encompass all government spending in Missouri. But even when we account for total government spending, including what comes from the U.S. government, it tells a similar story.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/7837ce85-4e22-41c8-845e-36546f2df94d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
5
The numbers don't line up perfectly with the "Income Tax as a % of Total Tax Revenue" chart above a) because of some small differences in definitions and b) because it was taken from a different year (2022 vs. 2025). Tax refund calculations factor in here as well. It doesn't change the overall story, but I wanted to address why there's a discrepancy.
6
Analysis from the Committee on Legislative Research says that eliminating the income tax will, by the time the repeal has been phased in, [cost the state more than $8.5 billion per year](https://substack.com/redirect/37caea64-b7be-4458-bddc-b6f279d494b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
7
It should be noted that the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy [is left-leaning](https://substack.com/redirect/5b3fc4a0-3500-4751-b999-5c09ed1b08fc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But more neutral organizations like the Tax Foundation [come to similar findings](https://substack.com/redirect/7a11e2a4-c8d6-4371-907d-aef490368fb6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and as a tax that's uniformly applied, it's definitionally going to be regressive.
8
Specifically, [24% is categorized as mandatory education spending](https://substack.com/redirect/8ca7489d-06a9-4447-ac9c-dd422452cf42?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and 50% as simply "Other Mandatories." [Amendment 5 prevents reductions in education spending](https://substack.com/redirect/73040f94-fcad-4061-a505-ef5ed4d7d2e5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), so that pool of money would be constitutionally untouchable, at least in theory.
9
My understanding here is that "mandatory" is spending required by law or by the state constitution, and "discretionary" refers to spending where the governor has more autonomy to allocate the budget. It shouldn't be taken to mean that the discretionary funding is optional, but its allocation may not be prescribed like it is for [state employee benefits](https://substack.com/redirect/3363dec3-3fb8-4c9b-a76b-348cba586521?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
10
Not actually important, but this ad is AI-produced in a way that puts it squarely in the [uncanny valley](https://substack.com/redirect/122b34f3-842c-4914-9d07-bd004df1707f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). They couldn't get real human actors to play knock-off NASCAR technicians? It looks like someone couldn't decide whether to make it look real or look like _Cars_ , so they landed somewhere in the middle.
11
Academic studies have tried to answer whether state-level income tax cuts are causally linked to economic growth. Different studies find different answers, but even studies that show a relationship between [state-level tax policy and growth say that it's relatively weak](https://substack.com/redirect/d5d1202a-9133-4aee-921d-e8b44da6e028?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Others find [no relationship between a state's tax rate and its economic growth rate](https://substack.com/redirect/81ad9c8b-8dd1-4c12-b364-210ed2c35b95?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
12
If you define educational attainment as "high school or higher," then [Missouri is above average](https://substack.com/redirect/83493cd5-7539-43cf-bdb1-e5b6a2d59146?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); if you define it as "bachelor's degree or higher," then Missouri is below average.
13
Looking at population growth since 2010: people like to point to Texas and Florida, which are indeed very fast-growing states that have no income tax. But Alaska and New Hampshire are relatively slow-growing states, and they also have no income tax. Meanwhile, Georgia, Idaho, and Montana are three of the country's fastest-growing states, and [they all have above-average tax rates](https://substack.com/redirect/1383502a-282f-4ff6-af41-0e6fd6b308be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

"Ceci n'est pas une sortie." Pretending there is a way to not use AI is an fiction you are using to excuse yourself from culpability. This image was made using AI. Claude Fable 5 wrote the prompt. ChatGPT 5.5 made the image. The author added the logo and the text using a font that mimics Magritte's "La Trahison des images" in Adobe Express.
_**by Lawrence Winnerman**_
My friend [Dana DuBois](https://open.substack.com/users/201342263-dana-dubois?utm_source=mentions) recently asked me if I knew the percentages behind how much active AI use there is versus how much passive AI use. She then wondered if she had maybe coined those terms--and while she's very good at coining terms, in this case, she didn't.
When I started doing research, I discovered that this point is fairly well discussed: the moments in our day when we actively choose AI--to generate an image, to organize our email, to outline a story we're writing--versus the moments when AI is fed to us by our phones, as in the summary of a text message breaking up with you before breakfast (just hypothetically speaking).
Sometimes the universe gives you hints about what it wants you to write next, and in this case mine came the next night at dinner.
While we were eating, another friend told me that she doesn't use AI at all.
She said it the way you'd mention you don't eat veal--quietly, without fanfare, with the settled calm of a person who has looked at a cruelty and stepped around it. She is not a foolish woman. She reads more than I do. She marches, she calls her representatives, she gives until it hurts. When she said it, the table murmured its approval, and somebody else said _me neither_ , and the conversation moved on to the salmon.
I didn't say anything. I want to tell you why, because the why is this essay.
I wanted what she said to be true. I had more reasons than anyone at that table to want it to be true. I was shoved out of a twenty-five-year career by the first wave of this technology, and then--because as every good GenXer who grew up singing "Blasphemous Rumours" knows, God has a sick sense of humor--I have recently been rebuilding my life by becoming the thing that shoved me out. [I have written before that I am the displaced and the displacer at once, and I have stopped expecting that sentence to get easier](https://substack.com/redirect/8ef99db9-6cc4-4a44-811d-3d68995a35f0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Nobody at that dinner wanted the exit she described to exist more than I did. A door out of the machine. A clean abstention. A way to be a bystander.
So I went looking for the door.
This essay is what I found.
Dear fellow human, I'm sorry in advance.
* * *
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/dcac0c8d-c83e-4ee7-858f-c48e393e1ee8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
#### **A Walk Through Tuesday**
Come with me through my friend's Tuesday. Not a hypothetical Tuesday--the ordinary one, the one she actually lived, the one any of us lived.
Her phone wakes her at 6:47, and before her feet find the floor she checks the weather, which is to say she consults a predictive model trained on decades of atmospheric data. She skims her email over coffee. She does not see the spam, because Gmail's machine learning reads on the order of fifteen billion unwanted messages a day and removes more than 99.9% of them before any human eye arrives--her mail was read by a machine this morning before it was read by her.
She buys the coffee with a tap of her card, and in the two hundred milliseconds before the terminal chirps, a model scores the transaction against everything Visa's systems know about fraud; those models blocked an estimated forty billion dollars of attempted theft in a single recent year. She drives to work along the blue line her map app draws, and the blue line is not a road. The blue line is a neural network's continuously revised guess about the future of traffic, based on real-time mobile-phone movement data, self-reported traffic incidents, and a thousand more variables.
At her desk she reads the news, and nearly every ad she scrolls past--about 90% of digital display advertising now--was placed by an algorithmic auction that identified her, valued her, and sold her attention in less time than a synapse takes to fire. There were hundreds of those auctions before lunch. She googled something at some point; roughly half of American queries now return an AI-composed answer above the results, which means the search engine did not point her at the machine. The search engine _was_ the machine.
Lunch is a scroll. More than half of what Instagram shows her is not from people she follows--it is conjured by a recommendation model that knows her tastes the way a river knows its bed. In the evening she watches something; more than 80% of the hours streamed on Netflix arrive through the recommender, and on YouTube the figure for recommendation-driven watch time runs around 70%. If music plays while she cooks, about three songs in ten were chosen for her by a model. Then she sleeps, and her Oura ring grades her sleep while the photos her phone took that day sort themselves by face, in the dark, while nobody watches.
She never opened a chatbot. Not once. She didn't generate an image of the president in diapers throwing a tantrum (for example). Her hands are clean.
And the machine was with her from 6:47 in the morning until she closed her eyes--reading her mail, pricing her attention, scoring her purchases, plotting her routes, choosing her evening. It never noticed her abstinence. There was nothing to notice. Abstinence happens at the front door, **and the machine does not use the front door.**
In late 2024, Gallup asked Americans about a week of their lives. Ninety-nine percent had used at least one AI-enabled product in the previous seven days--weather, streaming, navigation, social feeds, the ordinary furniture of a modern day. _**Sixty-four percent of those same people said they don 't use AI.**_
One of those numbers is a measurement. The other is a story we tell ourselves.
And the story has a strange shape when you hold it to the light. ChatGPT counts some nine hundred million weekly users now, _the fastest adoption curve of any product in history_ --and yet when Pew asked in 2025, only about a third of American adults had _ever_ used it.
Two-thirds of the country has never once touched the famous thing. Ninety-nine in a hundred swim daily in the quiet thing. We have built our entire moral conversation about AI around the famous thing, the thing with the text box and the name, the thing you can refuse--because the thing you can refuse is the only thing that lets you feel like you are making a choice.
As if the server asked you for your order, and you said, smugly, "_No AI for me, please. I 'm 100% human organic_."
Friend, unless you are somehow reading this from the year 1984, oh no, you most certainly are not.
* * *
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/dcac0c8d-c83e-4ee7-858f-c48e393e1ee8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
#### **The Buildings Don 't Care What You Believe**
[I have written before about the buildings--the windowless boxes humming behind berms off the interstate, the water they drink, the power they pull, the towns that wake up to find a cathedral of heat has moved in next door](https://substack.com/redirect/aa143aa5-1c43-4b72-8494-61e8abd2fa27?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). That essay was about what the buildings take. This one is about what they are.
Because here is what I assumed, and what I suspect my friend assumes: that there are AI buildings and internet buildings. That somewhere out there is the respectable old infrastructure--email, photos, movies, the family business of the web--and then, bolted on beside it, the new unclean annex where the chatbots live. Refuse the annex, keep the house. It is a reasonable picture.
It is also wrong, and it is wrong in a way that should rearrange your understanding of where you live.
As of early 2025, by Goldman Sachs's accounting, artificial intelligence accounted for about 14% of the power flowing through the world's data centers. The rest was everything else--the cloud at 54%, and at 32% the boring, beloved stack: your email, your backups, your photos of your kids, the enterprise software your job runs on, this essay, your quarterly business report slide deck, due next Wednesday.
The machine my friend thinks she is boycotting is a guest room in a house she has lived in for twenty years. Google's TPUs--the custom chips that trained Gemini--spent years serving YouTube and Maps before any of us had heard of a large language model. The same silicon. The same buildings. Satya Nadella, asked about Microsoft's build-out, reached for one word and said the goal was "fungibility of the fleet"--capacity that flows to whatever needs it, training run or Tuesday-night stream, with the building neither knowing nor caring which. The building was _designed_ not to care.
_Fungible silicon_ , agnostic to which electrons stream through it. (_Fungible silicon_ , by the way, is also my new band name.)
The industry has a name for the companies that own this machine--Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta--and for once the jargon tells the truth. They are called _hyperscalers_. The name is not a boast about size; it is a description of architecture. Hyperscale computing grows sideways: when demand spikes, nobody buys a bigger machine--they add ten thousand more identical cheap ones, and a layer of software stitches them into a single seamless organism that routes around failure without a human hand touching anything. When a server dies, nobody fixes it; the system simply stops sending it work and lets it go dark in its rack. Roughly half of the world's data center capacity now sits inside hyperscaler buildings, and the share is headed for two-thirds within five years. Hold the word, because the architecture is the argument: a machine deliberately built so that any workload can land on any chip is a machine with no separate rooms. There is no AI wing to boycott. There is no clean corridor to stand in.
And before you ask--yes, the new cathedrals are different. Abilene, Texas: 1.2 gigawatts rising for OpenAI--just shy of the 1.21 a flux capacitor needs--not to go back to the future, but to become part of a megacluster of servers. Memphis: two gigawatts and half a million GPUs behind xAI's fences. Meta's Hyperion in Louisiana, scaling toward five. These are temples built for one god, and no one's home movies will ever live there.
So which picture is true--the shared house or the dedicated temple? **Both.**
And that is precisely the trap. The internet you already live on runs through the shared machine, so your abstinence carries you through it anyway; and the temples run on capital and contracts, so your abstinence never touches them at all.
The door you refuse to walk through is not connected to either building.
There is one more thing the buildings know that we have not wanted to learn. Video--streaming, the thing we all do without a flicker of guilt--was 65% of all internet traffic as recently as 2022. It had been the heaviest thing online for a decade. And in that decade, global data center energy use barely moved: a 550% explosion in computing was absorbed with roughly a 6% rise in energy, a feat of efficiency documented in _**Science**_ in 2020 and noticed by approximately no one.
Nobody held a candlelight vigil for the YouTube servers. Nobody at any dinner party ever announced, gently, that they had given up streaming for the sake of the grid. The infrastructure only became legible to us--only became _moral terrain_ --when the machine started talking back.
I don't say that to absolve the new buildings; their bill is real, and I have itemized it elsewhere. [Their construction, paradoxically, is the only thing keeping the US economy out of a recession at the moment--a conundrum that melts your brain as soon as you start to think about how the AI that will one day run on them is coming for middle-class jobs](https://substack.com/redirect/bb2f7475-1f07-4da3-8f44-18b6adf541ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
I say it because it tells you what kind of objection we are actually making. We are not objecting to the machine. We were inside the machine for twenty years and called it convenience. We are objecting to the machine becoming _visible_ --and a visibility objection can be satisfied by making the machine invisible again, which is exactly what the fiction of opting out accomplishes.
Refusing to prompt a chatbot reduces the machine's load the way holding your breath fights climate change.
**You can do it, but it won 't help, and we actually need you to do something **_**more effective.**_
* * *
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/dcac0c8d-c83e-4ee7-858f-c48e393e1ee8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
#### **Active and Passive**
So let us name the thing properly, because if we can see it, we should be able to name it.
Active use is a verb. You open the tool, you type the words, you take the output, and you own the choice--every part of that is yours, refusable, accountable. Passive use is not a verb. Passive use is a tense. It is the condition your day is conjugated in: the filtered inbox, the scored swipe, the ranked feed, the routed drive, the auctioned attention. You do not _do_ passive use. You _live in_ it, the way you live in a climate. And nobody asks the climate's permission, and the climate does not ask yours.
In September 2025, Pew found that 62% of American adults knowingly interact with AI at least several times a week. The number that matters more is this one: 13% feel they have any real control over whether AI enters their lives at all.
Thirteen percent. Read that as a weather report, because that is what it is. Eighty-seven percent of the country, standing in the rain, being told the ethical question of our age is whether they choose to carry an umbrella.
I can hear the objection, and it deserves an answer rather than a wave. _You 're conflating things,_ a careful reader says. _A spam filter is not a chatbot. A recommender system is not a large language model. Predictive AI and generative AI are different technologies with different risks, and lumping them together is rhetorical sleight of hand._
The taxonomy is real, and I concede it without a fight.
But walk to the border between the categories and watch what is happening there--the border itself is moving, toward you and past you, even as you watch.
Google's search ranking has run on transformer language models--the same architecture as ChatGPT--since 2019. Gmail's newest spam filter _is_ a large language model. Mastercard now markets its fraud engine as generative AI. The membrane between the unclean technology and the ambient one is dissolving while we stand here arguing about which side of it we are on.
And there is an older law at work, one the computer scientists noticed generations ago and named the AI effect: _AI is whatever hasn 't been done yet._ The moment a model works--really works, reliably, at scale--we stop calling it AI and start calling it plumbing. The spell checker was AI once. The route planner was AI once. The thing reading your mail right now was AI until it became infallible, at which point it became infrastructure and vanished from the moral map. This is not an accident of language. Invisibility is the technology's final feature, the one that ships last. The system is at its most powerful exactly when it stops appearing on the list of things you believe you could refuse.
You can refuse a tool. You cannot refuse a tense.
* * *
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/dcac0c8d-c83e-4ee7-858f-c48e393e1ee8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
#### **The Footprint**
In 2004, the oil company BP--then mid-rebrand into "Beyond Petroleum," spending more than a hundred million dollars a year on the effort with the advertising firm Ogilvy & Mather--unveiled a small, friendly tool on its website. **It was called a carbon footprint calculator.** Find out how your daily life heats the planet, it offered. Go on a low-carbon diet. Two hundred seventy-eight thousand people used it in its first year. Before that campaign, the phrase "carbon footprint" barely existed; Google searches for it registered close to zero. The historian Benjamin Franta later gave the maneuver its proper name: a micro truth in a macro lie. The micro truth: your choices have a cost. The macro lie: that the ledger of a planetary crisis is kept in your kitchen, rather than in the boardrooms of the few dozen companies doing the extracting.
It worked. God help us, it worked for twenty years. An entire generation of decent people learned to audit their groceries while the wells ran wide open--learned to feel personally filthy and personally absolved in a cycle that never once approached the actual machinery. It was the most successful redirection of moral energy in the history of public relations.
I want you to look at the opt-out fiction until you see the same architecture. The question of artificial intelligence is a question of power--who builds the machine, who owns it, who profits, who decides where it lands and what it eats and whom it replaces, who pays when it is wrong. Every one of those questions has an address. And we have converted the whole stack of them into a different question entirely: _have you, personally, touched the unclean thing?_ Power has been swapped out for purity while we were busy feeling good.
And here is the detail that should keep us up at night: **this time, nobody had to spend a hundred million dollars to sell it to us.**
_**We did it to ourselves, for free.**_
The companies needed no Ogilvy. We looked at the largest concentration of infrastructural power in human history and we reached, unprompted, for the one response that has never built or stopped anything: personal cleanliness. Purity is so much easier than politics. Purity you can achieve alone, before lunch, without meetings. Politics requires the one thing the fiction quietly excuses you from: showing up with other people, again and again, for years.
Be fair to the impulse--I intend to be, because the impulse is decent and some of the people holding it are the best people I know. Underneath the abstention is solidarity with artists whose life's work was strip-mined without consent or payment. Underneath it is disgust at slop, and a refusal to applaud on command for a future being marketed as inevitable. Those are not poses; those are values, and in one narrow lane the refusal even finds a target--declining to generate AI images touches an actual product with an actual revenue line, and the artists are right to ask it of us. I honor all of it.
But an ethic that begins and ends with abstinence is not an ethic. It is hygiene. And clean hands have never once stopped a machine.
_**Clean hands are performative.**_
**Clean hands have never done the gritty work of a revolution --not in any age when power held the chains of enslavement and servitude.**
Meanwhile, the fiction does its quiet work. It produces the _feeling_ of resistance at none of resistance's costs--and the feeling is the harm, because the feeling metabolizes exactly the energy that organizing needs. Not one regulation has passed because a million people declined to make a chatbot write their emails. Not one data center has moved an inch for an empty text box. Not one moderator scrubbing the machine's nightmares for two dollars an hour in the Global South has gotten a raise out of anyone's abstinence.
And I can prove the energy works when it is pointed at something real, because data centers _are_ being stopped--just never by abstainers. In 2025 alone, organized neighbors--town boards, county commissions, ranchers and retirees packing rezoning hearings in rooms with bad fluorescent lighting--blocked or stalled at least forty-eight of them, $156 billion worth of buildout, and the pace has only quickened since: more than twenty more projects killed in the first quarter of this year. Communities in at least fourteen states have forced pauses on new construction; Maine is moving toward an outright ban; [Erin Brockovich](https://open.substack.com/users/1100053-erin-brockovich?utm_source=mentions) [keeps a map](https://substack.com/redirect/694ac4ce-b9fb-428a-ad3e-7350d6aabba3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). None of those people won by being pure. Most of them, I would wager, have ranked feeds and filtered inboxes like the rest of us.
They won by showing up, unclean, dripping with data, in a folding chair, at a Tuesday-night hearing.
The machine does not register your absence. The county commission does. The senator would.

* * *
There is a door on the wall of this moment, marked EXIT, and a long line of good people standing in front of it, feeling the freedom of knowing it is there.
**The door is painted on.**
I checked--that is what this essay was, the sound of me checking. The wall behind the paint is real, and it is load-bearing, and it goes up a gigawatt at a time whether we touch the text box or not. _The only way out has never been a door_. It is the slow, unglamorous work of deciding, together, what gets built into the wall--and that work has a thousand open seats and no purity requirement at all.
And one more thing, the thing I have been holding back all essay, the reason this is only one essay in this series. While we stand in the rich, mostly white world of the Global North admiring our painted door and grading one another's abstinence, the actual bill for this machine is being totaled somewhere else--in Manila at midnight, in Nairobi at two dollars an hour, in a drought-cracked valley in Chile where the cooling water used to be.
It is rolling downhill, the way the bill always rolls. And if you are one of the people in the folding chairs--**if the cathedral went up next to your county 's water--you already know the slope, because you live on it**. But the hill does not end at your property line. It keeps going, past the last American transmission tower, all the way down.
The next essay is about who lives at the bottom.
_**Spoiler alert: it probably isn 't you.**_

clean_body: 99% of Americans used AI last week. 64% of them swear they don't use it at all. One of those numbers is a measurement. The other is you doing the industry's work for free. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? 99% of Americans used AI last week. 64% of them swear they don't use it at all. One of those numbers is a measurement. The other is you doing the industry's work for free. | | and | Jun 11 | | | ---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- "Ceci n'est pas une sortie." Pretending there is a way to not use AI is an fiction you are using to excuse yourself from culpability. This image was made using AI. Claude Fable 5 wrote the prompt. ChatGPT 5.5 made the image. The author added the logo and the text using a font that mimics Magritte's "La Trahison des images" in Adobe Express. by Lawrence Winnerman My friend recently asked me if I knew the percentages behind how much active AI use there is versus how much passive AI use. She then wondered if she had maybe coined those terms--and while she's very good at coining terms, in this case, she didn't. When I started doing research, I discovered that this point is fairly well discussed: the moments in our day when we actively choose AI--to generate an image, to organize our email, to outline a story we're writing--versus the moments when AI is fed to us by our phones, as in the summary of a text message breaking up with you before breakfast (just hypothetically speaking). Sometimes the universe gives you hints about what it wants you to write next, and in this case mine came the next night at dinner. While we were eating, another friend told me that she doesn't use AI at all. She said it the way you'd mention you don't eat veal--quietly, without fanfare, with the settled calm of a person who has looked at a cruelty and stepped around it. She is not a foolish woman. She reads more than I do. She marches, she calls her representatives, she gives until it hurts. When she said it, the table murmured its approval, and somebody else said me neither , and the conversation moved on to the salmon. I didn't say anything. I want to tell you why, because the why is this essay. I wanted what she said to be true. I had more reasons than anyone at that table to want it to be true. I was shoved out of a twenty-five-year career by the first wave of this technology, and then--because as every good GenXer who grew up singing "Blasphemous Rumours" knows, God has a sick sense of humor--I have recently been rebuilding my life by becoming the thing that shoved me out. . Nobody at that dinner wanted the exit she described to exist more than I did. A door out of the machine. A clean abstention. A way to be a bystander. So I went looking for the door. This essay is what I found. Dear fellow human, I'm sorry in advance. | | ---|---|--- A Walk Through Tuesday Come with me through my friend's Tuesday. Not a hypothetical Tuesday--the ordinary one, the one she actually lived, the one any of us lived. Her phone wakes her at 6:47, and before her feet find the floor she checks the weather, which is to say she consults a predictive model trained on decades of atmospheric data. She skims her email over coffee. She does not see the spam, because Gmail's machine learning reads on the order of fifteen billion unwanted messages a day and removes more than 99.9% of them before any human eye arrives--her mail was read by a machine this morning before it was read by her. She buys the coffee with a tap of her card, and in the two hundred milliseconds before the terminal chirps, a model scores the transaction against everything Visa's systems know about fraud; those models blocked an estimated forty billion dollars of attempted theft in a single recent year. She drives to work along the blue line her map app draws, and the blue line is not a road. The blue line is a neural network's continuously revised guess about the future of traffic, based on real-time mobile-phone movement data, self-reported traffic incidents, and a thousand more variables. At her desk she reads the news, and nearly every ad she scrolls past--about 90% of digital display advertising now--was placed by an algorithmic auction that identified her, valued her, and sold her attention in less time than a synapse takes to fire. There were hundreds of those auctions before lunch. She googled something at some point; roughly half of American queries now return an AI-composed answer above the results, which means the search engine did not point her at the machine. The search engine was the machine. Lunch is a scroll. More than half of what Instagram shows her is not from people she follows--it is conjured by a recommendation model that knows her tastes the way a river knows its bed. In the evening she watches something; more than 80% of the hours streamed on Netflix arrive through the recommender, and on YouTube the figure for recommendation-driven watch time runs around 70%. If music plays while she cooks, about three songs in ten were chosen for her by a model. Then she sleeps, and her Oura ring grades her sleep while the photos her phone took that day sort themselves by face, in the dark, while nobody watches. She never opened a chatbot. Not once. She didn't generate an image of the president in diapers throwing a tantrum (for example). Her hands are clean. And the machine was with her from 6:47 in the morning until she closed her eyes--reading her mail, pricing her attention, scoring her purchases, plotting her routes, choosing her evening. It never noticed her abstinence. There was nothing to notice. Abstinence happens at the front door, and the machine does not use the front door. In late 2024, Gallup asked Americans about a week of their lives. Ninety-nine percent had used at least one AI-enabled product in the previous seven days--weather, streaming, navigation, social feeds, the ordinary furniture of a modern day. Sixty-four percent of those same people said they don 't use AI. One of those numbers is a measurement. The other is a story we tell ourselves. And the story has a strange shape when you hold it to the light. ChatGPT counts some nine hundred million weekly users now, the fastest adoption curve of any product in history --and yet when Pew asked in 2025, only about a third of American adults had ever used it. Two-thirds of the country has never once touched the famous thing. Ninety-nine in a hundred swim daily in the quiet thing. We have built our entire moral conversation about AI around the famous thing, the thing with the text box and the name, the thing you can refuse--because the thing you can refuse is the only thing that lets you feel like you are making a choice. As if the server asked you for your order, and you said, smugly, "No AI for me, please. I 'm 100% human organic." Friend, unless you are somehow reading this from the year 1984, oh no, you most certainly are not. | | ---|---|--- The Buildings Don 't Care What You Believe . That essay was about what the buildings take. This one is about what they are. Because here is what I assumed, and what I suspect my friend assumes: that there are AI buildings and internet buildings. That somewhere out there is the respectable old infrastructure--email, photos, movies, the family business of the web--and then, bolted on beside it, the new unclean annex where the chatbots live. Refuse the annex, keep the house. It is a reasonable picture. It is also wrong, and it is wrong in a way that should rearrange your understanding of where you live. As of early 2025, by Goldman Sachs's accounting, artificial intelligence accounted for about 14% of the power flowing through the world's data centers. The rest was everything else--the cloud at 54%, and at 32% the boring, beloved stack: your email, your backups, your photos of your kids, the enterprise software your job runs on, this essay, your quarterly business report slide deck, due next Wednesday. The machine my friend thinks she is boycotting is a guest room in a house she has lived in for twenty years. Google's TPUs--the custom chips that trained Gemini--spent years serving YouTube and Maps before any of us had heard of a large language model. The same silicon. The same buildings. Satya Nadella, asked about Microsoft's build-out, reached for one word and said the goal was "fungibility of the fleet"--capacity that flows to whatever needs it, training run or Tuesday-night stream, with the building neither knowing nor caring which. The building was designed not to care. Fungible silicon , agnostic to which electrons stream through it. (Fungible silicon , by the way, is also my new band name.) The industry has a name for the companies that own this machine--Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta--and for once the jargon tells the truth. They are called hyperscalers. The name is not a boast about size; it is a description of architecture. Hyperscale computing grows sideways: when demand spikes, nobody buys a bigger machine--they add ten thousand more identical cheap ones, and a layer of software stitches them into a single seamless organism that routes around failure without a human hand touching anything. When a server dies, nobody fixes it; the system simply stops sending it work and lets it go dark in its rack. Roughly half of the world's data center capacity now sits inside hyperscaler buildings, and the share is headed for two-thirds within five years. Hold the word, because the architecture is the argument: a machine deliberately built so that any workload can land on any chip is a machine with no separate rooms. There is no AI wing to boycott. There is no clean corridor to stand in. And before you ask--yes, the new cathedrals are different. Abilene, Texas: 1.2 gigawatts rising for OpenAI--just shy of the 1.21 a flux capacitor needs--not to go back to the future, but to become part of a megacluster of servers. Memphis: two gigawatts and half a million GPUs behind xAI's fences. Meta's Hyperion in Louisiana, scaling toward five. These are temples built for one god, and no one's home movies will ever live there. So which picture is true--the shared house or the dedicated temple? Both. And that is precisely the trap. The internet you already live on runs through the shared machine, so your abstinence carries you through it anyway; and the temples run on capital and contracts, so your abstinence never touches them at all. The door you refuse to walk through is not connected to either building. There is one more thing the buildings know that we have not wanted to learn. Video--streaming, the thing we all do without a flicker of guilt--was 65% of all internet traffic as recently as 2022. It had been the heaviest thing online for a decade. And in that decade, global data center energy use barely moved: a 550% explosion in computing was absorbed with roughly a 6% rise in energy, a feat of efficiency documented in Science in 2020 and noticed by approximately no one. Nobody held a candlelight vigil for the YouTube servers. Nobody at any dinner party ever announced, gently, that they had given up streaming for the sake of the grid. The infrastructure only became legible to us--only became moral terrain --when the machine started talking back. I don't say that to absolve the new buildings; their bill is real, and I have itemized it elsewhere. . I say it because it tells you what kind of objection we are actually making. We are not objecting to the machine. We were inside the machine for twenty years and called it convenience. We are objecting to the machine becoming visible --and a visibility objection can be satisfied by making the machine invisible again, which is exactly what the fiction of opting out accomplishes. Refusing to prompt a chatbot reduces the machine's load the way holding your breath fights climate change. You can do it, but it won 't help, and we actually need you to do something more effective. | | ---|---|--- Active and Passive So let us name the thing properly, because if we can see it, we should be able to name it. Active use is a verb. You open the tool, you type the words, you take the output, and you own the choice--every part of that is yours, refusable, accountable. Passive use is not a verb. Passive use is a tense. It is the condition your day is conjugated in: the filtered inbox, the scored swipe, the ranked feed, the routed drive, the auctioned attention. You do not do passive use. You live in it, the way you live in a climate. And nobody asks the climate's permission, and the climate does not ask yours. In September 2025, Pew found that 62% of American adults knowingly interact with AI at least several times a week. The number that matters more is this one: 13% feel they have any real control over whether AI enters their lives at all. Thirteen percent. Read that as a weather report, because that is what it is. Eighty-seven percent of the country, standing in the rain, being told the ethical question of our age is whether they choose to carry an umbrella. I can hear the objection, and it deserves an answer rather than a wave. You 're conflating things, a careful reader says. A spam filter is not a chatbot. A recommender system is not a large language model. Predictive AI and generative AI are different technologies with different risks, and lumping them together is rhetorical sleight of hand. The taxonomy is real, and I concede it without a fight. But walk to the border between the categories and watch what is happening there--the border itself is moving, toward you and past you, even as you watch. Google's search ranking has run on transformer language models--the same architecture as ChatGPT--since 2019. Gmail's newest spam filter is a large language model. Mastercard now markets its fraud engine as generative AI. The membrane between the unclean technology and the ambient one is dissolving while we stand here arguing about which side of it we are on. And there is an older law at work, one the computer scientists noticed generations ago and named the AI effect: AI is whatever hasn 't been done yet. The moment a model works--really works, reliably, at scale--we stop calling it AI and start calling it plumbing. The spell checker was AI once. The route planner was AI once. The thing reading your mail right now was AI until it became infallible, at which point it became infrastructure and vanished from the moral map. This is not an accident of language. Invisibility is the technology's final feature, the one that ships last. The system is at its most powerful exactly when it stops appearing on the list of things you believe you could refuse. You can refuse a tool. You cannot refuse a tense. | | ---|---|--- The Footprint In 2004, the oil company BP--then mid-rebrand into "Beyond Petroleum," spending more than a hundred million dollars a year on the effort with the advertising firm Ogilvy & Mather--unveiled a small, friendly tool on its website. It was called a carbon footprint calculator. Find out how your daily life heats the planet, it offered. Go on a low-carbon diet. Two hundred seventy-eight thousand people used it in its first year. Before that campaign, the phrase "carbon footprint" barely existed; Google searches for it registered close to zero. The historian Benjamin Franta later gave the maneuver its proper name: a micro truth in a macro lie. The micro truth: your choices have a cost. The macro lie: that the ledger of a planetary crisis is kept in your kitchen, rather than in the boardrooms of the few dozen companies doing the extracting. It worked. God help us, it worked for twenty years. An entire generation of decent people learned to audit their groceries while the wells ran wide open--learned to feel personally filthy and personally absolved in a cycle that never once approached the actual machinery. It was the most successful redirection of moral energy in the history of public relations. I want you to look at the opt-out fiction until you see the same architecture. The question of artificial intelligence is a question of power--who builds the machine, who owns it, who profits, who decides where it lands and what it eats and whom it replaces, who pays when it is wrong. Every one of those questions has an address. And we have converted the whole stack of them into a different question entirely: have you, personally, touched the unclean thing? Power has been swapped out for purity while we were busy feeling good. And here is the detail that should keep us up at night: this time, nobody had to spend a hundred million dollars to sell it to us. We did it to ourselves, for free. The companies needed no Ogilvy. We looked at the largest concentration of infrastructural power in human history and we reached, unprompted, for the one response that has never built or stopped anything: personal cleanliness. Purity is so much easier than politics. Purity you can achieve alone, before lunch, without meetings. Politics requires the one thing the fiction quietly excuses you from: showing up with other people, again and again, for years. Be fair to the impulse--I intend to be, because the impulse is decent and some of the people holding it are the best people I know. Underneath the abstention is solidarity with artists whose life's work was strip-mined without consent or payment. Underneath it is disgust at slop, and a refusal to applaud on command for a future being marketed as inevitable. Those are not poses; those are values, and in one narrow lane the refusal even finds a target--declining to generate AI images touches an actual product with an actual revenue line, and the artists are right to ask it of us. I honor all of it. But an ethic that begins and ends with abstinence is not an ethic. It is hygiene. And clean hands have never once stopped a machine. Clean hands are performative. Clean hands have never done the gritty work of a revolution --not in any age when power held the chains of enslavement and servitude. Meanwhile, the fiction does its quiet work. It produces the feeling of resistance at none of resistance's costs--and the feeling is the harm, because the feeling metabolizes exactly the energy that organizing needs. Not one regulation has passed because a million people declined to make a chatbot write their emails. Not one data center has moved an inch for an empty text box. Not one moderator scrubbing the machine's nightmares for two dollars an hour in the Global South has gotten a raise out of anyone's abstinence. And I can prove the energy works when it is pointed at something real, because data centers are being stopped--just never by abstainers. In 2025 alone, organized neighbors--town boards, county commissions, ranchers and retirees packing rezoning hearings in rooms with bad fluorescent lighting--blocked or stalled at least forty-eight of them, $156 billion worth of buildout, and the pace has only quickened since: more than twenty more projects killed in the first quarter of this year. Communities in at least fourteen states have forced pauses on new construction; Maine is moving toward an outright ban; . None of those people won by being pure. Most of them, I would wager, have ranked feeds and filtered inboxes like the rest of us. They won by showing up, unclean, dripping with data, in a folding chair, at a Tuesday-night hearing. The machine does not register your absence. The county commission does. The senator would. | | ---|---|--- There is a door on the wall of this moment, marked EXIT, and a long line of good people standing in front of it, feeling the freedom of knowing it is there. The door is painted on. I checked--that is what this essay was, the sound of me checking. The wall behind the paint is real, and it is load-bearing, and it goes up a gigawatt at a time whether we touch the text box or not. The only way out has never been a door. It is the slow, unglamorous work of deciding, together, what gets built into the wall--and that work has a thousand open seats and no purity requirement at all. And one more thing, the thing I have been holding back all essay, the reason this is only one essay in this series. While we stand in the rich, mostly white world of the Global North admiring our painted door and grading one another's abstinence, the actual bill for this machine is being totaled somewhere else--in Manila at midnight, in Nairobi at two dollars an hour, in a drought-cracked valley in Chile where the cooling water used to be. It is rolling downhill, the way the bill always rolls. And if you are one of the people in the folding chairs--if the cathedral went up next to your county 's water--you already know the slope, because you live on it. But the hill does not end at your property line. It keeps going, past the last American transmission tower, all the way down. The next essay is about who lives at the bottom. Spoiler alert: it probably isn 't you. Cliff 's Note: Look. My partner in crime at Blue Amp, Lawrence Winnerman, just published the essay I'll be quoting at dinner parties for a year. You "don't use AI"? Buddy. It read your email, scored your card swipe, and picked your evening before you finished your coffee. 99% of Americans used AI last week. 64% swear they didn't. That exit door you're so proud of standing in front of? Painted on. The predator class is counting on you feeling pure instead of getting organized. Read it. Then go paid--40% off right now. ---
| | Dear Peter,
Kshama for Congress volunteers and rank-and-file union members will be at the Labor Notes convention in Chicago this upcoming weekend, Friday, June 12th through Sunday, June 14th!
---
| | **If you are planning to attend Labor Notes, please find us and attend our Kshama for Congress Labor Meetup!**
**Saturday, June 13th, at 6:30PM****after the day’s panel discussions.**
**We will meet at the entry level foyer.****Email us at campaign@kshamasawant.org**
---
| | Tens of thousands of workers and rank-and-file union members across the country support Kshama’s revolutionary socialist campaign. **They want to fight the rich, not their wars.** They want free healthcare by taxing the rich, a massive expansion of social housing, and an end to the imperialist wars and the genocide in Gaza. Union members want strong contracts with real wage increases and protections against AI layoffs. Non-unionized workers want to fight to unionize their workplaces and win strong contracts.
**They want to elect a FIGHTER to Congress, NOT another “team player”** for the Democratic or Republican parties.
The vast majority of the leadership in the labor movement right now is business unionist. These leaders have made peace with the capitalist system and the political parties of the capitalist class. Business unionist leaders do not want to organize rank-and-file union members into battles against the bosses. Making peace with the bosses also means being intertwined with the parties of the bosses. The American labor leadership today is, for the most part, glued to the Democratic Party. There is a revolving door among business unionist labor leaders, NGO leaders, Democratic Party politicians and operatives, and even individuals working directly for the bosses. Rather than organizing powerful strike actions to shut down the profit machine of the bosses to stop the genocide and wars, to win real gains like universal public healthcare and publicly-owned affordable housing, and to stop the hyperscale data centers and AI layoffs, we have labor leaders cheerleading a genocidal anti-worker party of the bosses.
All of this has meant that the billionaires have become unimaginably wealthy from war profiteering and exploiting tens of millions of American and immigrant workers. Most working people, including many union rank-and-file, are barely able to pay their rent and put food on the table.
---
| | **We need a reckoning in the labor movement.**
---
| | Our campaign has been canvassing throughout Congressional District 9 in Washington state. We have spoken to tens of thousands of working people, including hundreds of rank-and-file union members, in our district. They strongly agree with the demands that Kshama is running on:
* Free healthcare for all funded by taxing the rich
* End the genocide in Gaza, end all military aid to Israel, and end all weapons and tech for genocide and imperialist war
* A public-sector living-wage jobs guarantee, funded by taxing the rich
* The right to unionize for all workers
* National rent control and a massive expansion of publicly-owned affordable housing
* Stop the AI data centers and mass layoffs
* Shut down ICE and the detention centers
* A $25 an hour federal minimum wage, which should be higher in major cities

Kshama has widespread and strong support for these demands from workers and union members across all 50 states.
Kshama’s main opponent is 29-year incumbent Democratic Congressmember Adam Smith.
Adam Smith
* Has voted to send tens of billions of dollars for the Gaza genocide
* Has funded endless bloody wars for nearly three decades, including the war on Iraq
* Has championed a new trillion-dollar war budget this month on top of having cheerled $906 billion for war last December, money that Trump has used for the war on Iran
* Is bankrolled by the war profiteering billionaire class and the Zionist lobby
* Has voted to create and fund ICE
* Slashed hundreds of billions of dollars from Medicare and Medicaid
* Condemned antiwar protesters as “left-wing fascists” and demanded they be arrested
* Voted to bail out Wall Street in the wake of the 2008 Great Recession
* Voted to break the railroad workers’ strike in 2022

Any one of these horrific actions by a politician, including breaking a workers’ strike, should automatically disqualify them from labor support. **Yet, the leadership of the Washington State Labor Council, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) Council 28, the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE), and the National Education Association have all endorsed Adam Smith for Congress.**
Kshama’s decade-long track record as the independent socialist on the Seattle City Council stands in stark contrast to Adam Smith’s shockingly anti-working-class, pro-war, and pro-billionaire career. Kshama used her office to build mass movements of workers and union members to win the nation’s highest minimum wage, a historic movement that has resulted in tens of millions of workers nationally winning substantial wage increases. She took on Jeff Bezos and other billionaires and won the historic Amazon Tax that taxes the city’s wealthiest corporations and raises hundreds of millions of dollars annually to fund affordable housing. Kshama organized working-class renters, including union members, and defeated corporate landlords to win unprecedented renters’ rights, including the move-in fee cap and payment plan, which members of the Seattle Education Association played an important role in winning alongside her office. In November 2023, Kshama won the nation’s strongest City Council resolution against what has become the genocide in Gaza. She also won an important resolution in 2015 in solidarity with SEA’s strike at the time, something you never hear politicians doing! Kshama is a former teacher and member of the AFT Local 1789. As an elected representative, Kshama took home only the average worker’s wage and donated the rest of her six-figure City Council salary, after taxes, to labor strike funds and social movements.
Instead of continuing to use the shameful business unionist approach of so many labor leaders today, we need a fighting, class struggle approach, and a real fight back against the bosses. Unions need to break from both billionaire-backed parties entirely, and independent campaigns like ours are a crucial part of that process.
**Electing Kshama to Congress would be a massive boost to class struggle unionism across the country.**
Kshama’s first election as an independent socialist to the Seattle City Council 2013 became a referendum on the demand for a $15/hour minimum wage because Kshama used the campaign itself as a vehicle to build momentum for 15, not her own career. At the time, the business unionist labor leaders refused to support it. But after Kshama won, she immediately launched the 15 NOW movement, which mobilized hundreds of workers and union members in the city, forcing the labor leadership to join the fight. Less than six months after Kshama took office, she had won the historic wage increase alongside Seattle’s working class. If Kshama is elected, she will bring that class-struggle, fighting strategy onto the national level. **This is a rare opportunity to send a proven revolutionary working-class fighter to Congress!** Kshama has pledged that if elected, she will turn her Congressional inauguration into a mass rally of 10,000 people in Washington D.C., and immediately use her office to launch movements, and organize rank-and-file union members as a part of those movements, to end the Gaza genocide, end all military aid to Israel, and win free healthcare for all funded by taxing the rich.
Again, if you are attending Labor Notes this weekend, please find our campaign volunteers this weekend!
---
| | **Please find us at Labor Notes and attend our****Kshama for Congress Labor Meetup!**
**Saturday, June 13th, at 6:30PM****after the day’s panel discussions.**
**We will meet at the entry level foyer.****Email us at campaign@kshamasawant.org**
**We will also be prepared to film individual endorsements for our social media, so please come prepared with some words about why you are supporting our independent, pro-worker, anti-war campaign.**

---
| | Regardless of whether you plan to attend Labor Notes, please sign up to volunteer and donate to our campaign!
Solidarity,Kshama for Congress

On May 9, Senator Rand Paul told the graduating class of Grove City College that the case for the future is a case for optimism, and a good part of that case was about artificial intelligence. He urged a hall full of new graduates not to be afraid of it. I think he was right, and I want to make that same case to my fellow Mississippians.
Two hundred years ago, English textile workers we now call the Luddites began smashing the new power looms, certain the machines would destroy them. They were skilled craftsmen, not fools, and they were still wrong. The looms won. The descendants of the Luddites did not end up poorer than their ancestors. They ended up with shorter workdays, longer lives, and work the loom-smashers could never have pictured. Every wave of technology since has run the same course. The fear is always sincere. The fear is almost always wrong.
Artificial intelligence is going to be part of life in Mississippi whether any one of us votes for it or not. The only question still in our hands is a personal one. Will you treat this thing as a threat to hide from, or as a tool to pick up? The people who get left behind by a new technology are rarely the ones who used it. They are the ones who refused to.
And this is a tool everyday Mississippians can use today. A row-crop farmer in the Delta can use AI to read soil and satellite data, time his planting and harvest, and flag a piece of equipment that is about to fail before it quits in the middle of a field. The owner of a two-person business in Tupelo or Meridian can use it to draft her marketing, answer routine customer emails, and get a plain-English read on a contract before she signs it. A schoolteacher can build lesson plans and write three versions of one assignment for students reading at three different levels. A nurse in a rural clinic can speed up the charting that consumes her shift, so more of her day is spent facing a patient instead of a keyboard. These are not science-fiction examples. People in those jobs are doing this right now.
I want to be honest about the real worry, because Senator Paul was. A world with no meaningful work at all would be its own kind of dystopia. Work is part of how human beings find purpose. But embracing AI does not mean a future with no work. It means less drudgery and more of the work that actually mattered in the first place.
Here is why this matters for Mississippi. Our state has spent most of my lifetime being last. Last to get the factory, last to get the investment, last to catch the wave of prosperity that lifted other states first. This time we do not have to be last. These tools are not locked behind a Silicon Valley zip code. A teacher in Senatobia and a teacher in San Francisco can open the very same AI tool tonight. For once in our history, the playing field is close to level.
The technology is not waiting for our permission. So the question for every Mississippian is the one Senator Paul put to those graduates. Will you meet the future with fear, or with curiosity and a plan? Here is a plan small enough to start this week. Find one task in your work or your home where AI could save you an hour. Just one. Use it. Then do it again next week. That is how you make sure you are not the one left behind. Not by fighting the future, but by deciding to be one of the people who picked up the tool.
